doc.title: Joe LaBarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 15, 2021

title: Learning drums from stock arrangements, then clarinet and sax
summary: Stock drum parts in the style of Baby Dodds, father singing rhythms, starting drums at five, then clarinet and saxophone and what that gave his melodic sense.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: When he — he had stock arrangements for a lot of the things that you did. Were there drum parts and were you expected to follow them?

No. I mean there were drum parts, Monk, but if you look at any of those stocks from the 30s, the drum part really, what’s designated for playing time is basically four quarter notes connected by rolls, and four beats on the bass drum. You know that’s kind of a ballpark approximation of what, you know, Baby Dodds would have played or any of the early drummers, you know, that kind of real — nothing on the ride cymbal. There was no ride cymbal. It was all about playing the time on the snare drum. So I started out playing in that style of Baby Dodds.
What if someone wanted to do a rumba? Would your father have vocalized the beat to you? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Yes. He would have sung it to me, play it like this, and then I would do my best to imitate it.
Okay. And the drums wasn’t the only part of your musical education, am I correct? Like you played a clarinet and sax a bit?

That’s correct. I started drums at five, and then by the time I was seven I think or eight, my embouchure had fully formed so I took up the clarinet and then that was followed by the saxophone. And I played that all through high school.
I see. I think that must have paid some dividends down the road when you decided that you wanted to compose also, would that be —

That’s true, Monk, sorry I didn’t mean to interrupt you. It also paid the most dividend when I was starting to improvise with other musicians and I had that melodic sense kind of ingrained into my head about what music is supposed to sound like. You know I could almost visualize the perspective of the saxophone player as that person would relate to the drummer. You know?
